layoutProps.lead: Green coffee keeps for months: that is how it crosses oceans. See what a buyer checks before a lot is shipped.

props.text: A year in the life of one lot

items.title: The shrubs flower
items.markdown: After the first heavy rains, the shrubs flower white for a few days, with a scent close to jasmine. Every cherry of the harvest comes from these flowers.

items.title: The harvest
items.markdown: The cherries ripen over weeks and the pickers pass every week or two. Processing starts within hours of picking.

items.title: Drying and resting
items.markdown: The beans dry for two to four weeks, then rest in their parchment for a month or more, so that their moisture evens out.

items.title: Milling and grading
items.markdown: The dry mill hulls and sorts the beans. A grader counts the defects in a sample, and the lot is roasted lightly and tasted.

items.title: At sea, then roasted
items.markdown: The sacks cross the ocean in a few weeks. Our roaster tastes the arrival sample, then roasts the lot for our cafés.

props.markdown: About 10 to 12 % of the bean's weight. Wetter beans can grow mould; drier ones age fast and taste flat.
A grader spreads a 350 g sample on a tray and counts what is wrong in it: black, broken or bitten beans, stones.
Last, a sample is roasted lightly and tasted, or *cupped*, to score its flavour and catch any fault.

props.alt: A dark tray holding a sample of green coffee beans, a few of them damaged or out of place.
props.prompt: Find what the grader pulls out of this sample.

items.title: A black bean
items.markdown: Dark all through: the cherry died on the shrub or fermented too long. A single one counts as a full defect, because it can give a whole cup a dirty, bitter taste.

items.title: A broken bean
items.markdown: Cracked by the huller. Pieces roast faster than whole beans and scorch, which adds bitterness.

items.title: Insect damage
items.markdown: Small holes left by the coffee berry borer, a beetle that lays its eggs in the cherry. A few are tolerated; many make the cup dull or sour.

items.title: A stone
items.markdown: Picked up on the drying patio. It tastes of nothing, but it can break a grinder: graders count it heavily.

props.stem: Which of these beans would a grader pull from the sample?

options.feedback: This is a peaberry: one round seed instead of two flat ones. It is not a defect; mills often sort peaberries out and sell them apart.
options.alt: A round green bean with a cut running along it.

options.feedback: A flat, even bean with a clean centre cut is exactly what the grader hopes to see.
options.alt: A flat, oval green bean with a clean, even centre cut.

options.feedback: Yes: a black bean is a full defect. One can taint a whole cup.
options.alt: A flat bean, dark brown to black all through.

props.alt: A metal scoop of pale green coffee beans over an open jute sack.
props.markdown: Dried to about 11 % moisture and kept in its jute sack, often with a sealed bag inside, green coffee stays fresh for months. Roasted coffee goes stale within weeks. So coffee crosses the ocean green, and is roasted close to where it is drunk.
